summary: This standards-track RFC describes multi-segment pseudowire protection scenarios in which redundancy is provided at the Switching Provider Edge. It specifies how the S-PEs operate and how the preferential forwarding status is signaled between them.

eli5.summary: If a relay point on a path breaks, a spare relay point can take over. This explains how they agree which one is in charge.

questions: what is the preferential forwarding status bit
subtitle: Letting a middle router of a multi-segment pseudowire pick between redundant paths, without changing the edge devices.

tldr.problem: In a multi-segment pseudowire, redundancy is normally handled end to end by the terminating edge routers. That burdens access nodes that may not support it and switches over more slowly.
tldr.mechanism: The switching router (S-PE) in the middle acts as Slave toward its single neighbour and Independent toward its several neighbours. It reuses the existing Preferential Forwarding status bit to choose the active segment.
tldr.outcome: Protection happens at the S-PE, needs no change to the terminating routers (T-PEs), and can switch faster than end-to-end protection.

today: RFC 7795 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2016, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6870 and RFC 6478.

sections.title: Why Redundancy at the S-PE
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries a link-layer service across a packet network. A multi-segment pseudowire (MS-PW) is built from several PW segments joined end to end. The routers at the two ends are Terminating Provider Edges (T-PEs), and the routers that join segments in the middle are Switching Provider Edges (S-PEs).

RFC 6718 gives the framework for PW redundancy and RFC 6870 specifies a mechanism for redundant PWs between PE nodes or between T-PEs. RFC 7795 covers the case where the redundancy is provided on the S-PE instead.

The RFC names two benefits: it reduces the burden on the access T-PE nodes, and it enables faster protection switching than end-to-end MS-PW protection. It does not require any change to the T-PEs.
sections.eli5: Instead of making the first runner in a relay keep track of backup runners, the runner in the middle keeps the spare. That is less work for the first runner and quicker when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Single-Homed and Multi-Homed Sides
sections.content:
An S-PE connects to its neighbouring T-PEs or S-PEs with PW segments. For an S-PE that provides PW redundancy for an MS-PW, there is a single PW segment on one side, called the single-homed side. On the other side there are multiple PW segments, called the multi-homed side.

The case where an S-PE has two multi-homed sides is out of scope.
sections.eli5: On one side of the middle runner there is one teammate. On the other side there are two or more, and the middle runner picks among them.

sections.title: The Two Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes two typical layouts. In the first, CE1 connects to T-PE1, T-PE1 connects only to S-PE1, and S-PE1 connects to both T-PE2 and T-PE3. CE2 is dual-homed to T-PE2 and T-PE3. The MS-PW is switched on S-PE1, and the segments PW-Seg2 and PW-Seg3 give resiliency against failure of T-PE2, T-PE3 or the attached Attachment Circuits (ACs). PW-Seg2 is the primary segment and PW-Seg3 the secondary.

In the second scenario, T-PE1 connects to both S-PE1 and S-PE2, and both S-PEs connect to both T-PE2 and T-PE3. Two MS-PWs are switched at S-PE1 and S-PE2 respectively, which adds protection against failure of an S-PE node. PW1 is the primary MS-PW and PW2 the secondary.

In the first scenario, the number of PW segments needed between T-PE1 and S-PE1 is only half of what end-to-end MS-PW redundancy would need. In the second, S-PE redundancy reduces the number of end-to-end MS-PWs required for both T-PE and S-PE protection.
sections.eli5: In the simple layout, one middle helper has two backup paths on the far side. In the bigger layout there are two middle helpers, so even if a whole helper breaks, the other one carries on.

sections.title: S-PE Operations
sections.content:
The S-PE MUST work in Slave mode for the single-homed side and in Independent mode for the multi-homed side. As a result, the T-PE on the single-homed side MUST work in Master mode, and the T-PEs on the multi-homed side MUST work in Independent mode. The Preferential Forwarding bit signaling of RFC 6870 and RFC 6478 is reused.

  • The S-PE MUST pass the Preferential Forwarding status received from the single-homed side, unchanged, to all PW segments on the multi-homed side.
  • The S-PE MUST advertise Standby to the single-homed side if it receives Standby from all multi-homed segments, and MUST advertise Active if it receives Active from any of them.
  • On the multi-homed side, the segment whose local and remote Up/Down status are both Up and whose local and remote Preferential Forwarding status are both Active MUST be selected for forwarding.

On the single-homed side, the active segment is chosen by the T-PE in Master mode. After a switchover, an S-PE that supports SP-PE TLV processing as defined in RFC 6073 SHOULD advertise updated SP-PE TLVs in a Label Mapping message to the T-PEs.

The optional S-PE Bypass mode of RFC 6478 MUST NOT be used here. Otherwise the S-PE would not receive the PW status messages originated by the T-PEs.
sections.eli5: The middle helper does what the first runner says about which lane is in use, and tells every backup lane the same thing. Toward the first runner it says it is ready if any backup lane is ready.

sections.title: Worked Failure Examples
sections.content:
In scenario 1, assume the AC from CE2 to T-PE2 is active. S-PE1 receives Active from T-PE1 and advertises Active on both PW-Seg2 and PW-Seg3. T-PE2 advertises Active and T-PE3 advertises Standby, so PW-Seg2 carries traffic.

If the AC between CE2 and T-PE2 fails, T-PE3 becomes Active and T-PE2 sends a PW status Notification saying the AC is down. S-PE1 switches to PW-Seg3. It still has an Active segment on the multi-homed side, so it does not advertise any PW status change to T-PE1.

In scenario 2, T-PE1 in Master mode advertises Active to S-PE1 and Standby to S-PE2, so S-PE1 carries traffic on PW1-Seg2. If S-PE1 itself fails, T-PE1 notices through some detection mechanism and advertises Active to S-PE2. S-PE2 then advertises Active to T-PE2 and T-PE3, and PW2-Seg2 is selected for forwarding.
sections.eli5: If one backup path breaks, the middle helper quietly switches to the other one and the first runner never notices. If a whole helper breaks, the first runner switches to the other helper.

sections.title: VCCV Considerations
sections.content:
For PW Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV, RFC 5085), control channel type 1 "PW ACH" can be used with this mechanism. Type 2 "Router Alert Label" is not supported for MS-PW as specified in RFC 6073.

If type 3 "TTL Expiry" is used, the PW label TTL MUST be set to the appropriate value to reach the target PE. The hop count from a T-PE to the target PE can come from SP-PE TLVs, MS-PW path trace, or management-plane information.
sections.eli5: There are special test messages to check the path works. Some kinds work here, one kind does not, and another needs the right hop count set.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Because redundancy is provided on the S-PE nodes of MS-PWs, it is important that the security mechanisms defined in RFC 4447, RFC 6073 and RFC 6478 be implemented. The goal is to ensure that the S-PE nodes, and the messages they send and receive, are not compromised. The RFC defines no new security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: The middle helper is trusted with an important job, so the safety rules from earlier documents must be used to keep it and its messages from being tampered with.
